questions.question: What are blocks and yield in Ruby?
questions.title: Ruby Blocks and Yield
questions.direct_answer: A block is an unnamed chunk of code you pass to a method, written with braces {} (one-liners) or do/end (multi-line): [1,2,3].each { |n| puts n }. A method calls the block with yield — yield runs the block, and yield(value) passes a value to it. The block is what makes iterators like each and map work: the method does the looping, and yield hands each element to the block you provide. You can check block_given? before yielding, and a block turns a method into a custom iterator without writing the loop yourself.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know blocks ({}/do-end), yield runs the block and passes values, and block_given? guards yield.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting block_given? (NoMethodError if no block), or confusing yield (calls block) with return.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: A block is an unnamed chunk passed to a method ({}/do-end); yield runs it and passes values. block_given? guards yield. This is how each/map work.

A method calls the block with yield — yield runs the block, and yield of value passes a value to it. You can check block given question mark before yielding to avoid an error when no block is given, and a block turns a method into a custom iterator without writing the loop yourself — that's the whole point of Ruby's iterator style. A common mistake is forgetting block given, because yield with no block raises LocalJumpError, and confusing yield, which calls the block, with return, which exits the method.

sections.title: Method -> yield -> Block
sections.content:
The method loops and yields each value; the block receives it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M[method loops] --> Y[yield value]
  Y --> B[block runs with value]
  B --> N[next value or done]
```

sections.title: Blocks and yield
sections.content:
```ruby
# Block with braces (one-liner):
[1, 2, 3].each { |n| puts n }   # prints 1 2 3

# Block with do/end (multi-line):
[1, 2, 3].each do |n|
  puts n * 2
end

# yield in your own method:
def repeat(n)
  n.times { yield }      # run the block n times
end
repeat(3) { puts 'hi' }  # hi hi hi

# yield with a value, and guard with block_given?:
def each_twice(arr)
  return enum_for(:each_twice, arr) unless block_given?
  arr.each { |x| yield x; yield x }   # pass x to the block
end
each_twice([1, 2]) { |v| puts v }   # 1 1 2 2
```
